13.3 Obesity.summary: Obesity is a risk factor for hypertension, coronary artery disease (CAD) and heart failure (HF), with a possibly stronger association with HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). An 'obesity paradox' has been described where overweight or mildly/moderately obese HF patients may have better prognosis than leaner patients; this paradox is not consistently observed in patients with diabetes. Body mass index (BMI) has limitations because it does not account for body composition; waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio may better reflect visceral obesity and outcomes.
diagnostic_notes: Obese patients with HF can have lower natriuretic peptide (NP) concentrations due to increased expression of clearance receptors and augmented peptide degradation by adipose tissue.
Peak oxygen consumption adjusted for body weight underestimates exercise capacity in obese patients; adjust for lean body mass for risk stratification.
clinical_implications: Consider measures beyond BMI (e.g., waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio) when assessing obesity-related risk.
Recognize altered biomarker (NP) levels in obese HF patients which may affect diagnosis and prognosis.
therapeutic_recommendations: Caloric restriction plus exercise training showed additive beneficial effects on exercise capacity and quality of life in obese patients with HFpEF in a randomized trial.
Interventions should consider preserving skeletal muscle mass; obese but fit patients with preserved muscle mass have better prognosis than sarcopenic obese patients.
notes_and_uncertainties: The obesity paradox may be influenced by confounders and is not universally seen across all subgroups (e.g., patients with diabetes).

13.4 Frailty, cachexia, sarcopenia.summary: Frailty is a multidimensional, dynamic condition increasing vulnerability to stressors and is common in HF. Frailty and HF are distinct but commonly coexisting; frailty is associated with worse outcomes and reduced treatment tolerance. Cachexia is a complex metabolic syndrome with loss of muscle (with or without fat loss) and is characterized clinically by >5% oedema-free body weight loss over the previous 12 months.
epidemiology: Frailty prevalence in HF patients may be up to 45% (meta-analysis cited).
Patients with HF are up to six times more likely to be frail than the general population.
Cachexia may occur in approximately 5–15% of patients with HF, particularly in HFrEF and advanced disease.
associated_risks: Frailty increases risk of death, hospitalizations, functional decline, and longer hospital stay.
Frailty and cachexia are linked to poorer outcomes and reduced tolerance/access to treatments.
assessment_and_tools: Assessment of frailty in HF is crucial. The Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the ESC developed an HF-specific frailty tool based on four major domains: clinical, psycho-cognitive, functional, and social.
management_recommendations: Treatment of frailty in HF should be multifactorial and targeted to main components.
Include physical rehabilitation with exercise training, nutritional supplementation, and individualized approaches to comorbidities.
cachexia_specifics: Defined as a complex metabolic syndrome associated with underlying illness and characterized by loss of muscle with or without fat mass.
Major clinical feature: >5% oedema-free body weight loss in prior 12 months (or equivalent criteria cited).
Cachexia may coexist with frailty and is more common in advanced HF/HFrEF.
